name: Running Student
description: A student is on a bus moving along the positive x-axis at a constant speed `vb`. The bus starts at (0,0) and makes `n` stops at coordinates `(xi, 0)`. The student needs to reach a university located at `(xu, yu)` and can run at a constant speed `vs`. The goal is to find the optimal bus stop to get off at (from the 2nd to the nth) to minimize the total travel time. Total time is the bus travel time to the stop plus the student's running time from the stop to the university. If times are equal, choose the stop closer to the university.

constraints.stop_coordinates_x: 0 <= xi <= 10^5, x1 is guaranteed to be 0.

input_spec.line_1: Three space-separated integers: `n` (number of stops), `vb` (bus speed), `vs` (student speed).
input_spec.line_2: `n` space-separated non-negative integers in ascending order: x-coordinates of the bus stops.
input_spec.line_3: Two space-separated integers: `xu`, `yu` (coordinates of the university).

output_spec.description: A single integer: the index (1-based) of the optimal bus stop to get off at.

notes: The student cannot get off at the first bus stop (index 1).
Time to get to stop `i` is `xi / vb`.
Time to run from stop `i` is `sqrt((xu-xi)^2 + yu^2) / vs`.
The tie-breaking rule is to choose the bus stop with the minimum Euclidean distance to the university.

examples.title: Problem Example 1
examples.why_included: This is the first example from the problem statement, a basic case where the optimal stop is in the middle.

examples.title: Problem Example 2
examples.why_included: This is the second example, which also tests maximum coordinate values and the minimum number of stops.

examples.title: Minimum Number of Stops (n=2)
examples.why_included: Tests the minimum `n` constraint. With only two stops, the only possible choice is the second stop.

examples.title: Maximum Number of Stops (n=100)
examples.why_included: Tests the maximum `n` constraint. Requires iterating through all possible stops.

examples.title: University Directly Above a Bus Stop
examples.why_included: The university's x-coordinate matches a bus stop's coordinate. The optimal stop is likely near this point.

examples.title: University on Bus Route (y=0)
examples.why_included: A special case where the university lies on the same line as the bus stops, simplifying distance calculations.

examples.title: Bus Much Faster Than Student
examples.why_included: When the bus is extremely fast, it's almost always optimal to stay on until the last stop.

examples.title: Student Much Faster Than Bus
examples.why_included: When the student is extremely fast, it's almost always optimal to get off at the first possible stop (stop 2).

examples.title: Tie-Breaker Case with Equal Times
examples.why_included: A specifically constructed case where two stops yield identical travel times. The tie must be broken by choosing the stop closer to the university.

examples.title: University at a Negative X-Coordinate
examples.why_included: Tests handling of negative university coordinates. The student should get off early as the bus moves away from the university.

examples.title: University Far Away (Large Y)
examples.why_included: When the university is very far vertically, the x-component of the running distance becomes less important, but the bus travel time still accumulates. This tests if the logic correctly balances these factors.

examples.title: Floating Point Precision Test
examples.why_included: This case is designed so that the total times for stops 2 and 3 are very close, requiring accurate floating-point arithmetic to distinguish the minimum.

examples.title: University at Negative Y Coordinate
examples.why_included: Tests handling of negative university coordinates. The result should be symmetric with a positive y-coordinate due to the distance formula using y^2.

examples.title: University at Origin (0,0)
examples.why_included: The student starts at the university. Since they must take the bus and can't get off at stop 1, the optimal choice is to get off at the very next stop (index 2) to minimize travel time.

examples.title: Clear Tie-Breaker by Distance
examples.why_included: A constructed case where stops 2 and 3 result in the exact same total travel time. The tie must be broken by choosing the stop physically closer to the university (stop 3).

examples.title: All Constraints at Maximum Values
examples.why_included: A stress test using maximum allowed values for n, speeds, and coordinates to check for performance and potential overflow with large numbers.

examples.title: Minimum Speeds (vb=1, vs=1)
examples.why_included: Tests with the slowest possible speeds, making travel times large. The logic should be to minimize `x_i + distance`.

examples.title: University Far Past the Last Stop
examples.why_included: When the university's x-coordinate is far beyond the last bus stop, the optimal strategy is always to take the bus to the very end.

examples.title: University Between First and Second Stops
examples.why_included: When the university is located before the second possible stop, the best choice must be that second stop to minimize backtracking.

examples.title: Precision Test with Small Y Value
examples.why_included: When `y_u` is very small, the running distance is almost horizontal. This creates very small differences in total time for stops near `x_u`, testing floating point precision.

examples.title: Densely Packed Bus Stops
examples.why_included: With stops very close to each other, the change in total time is minimal between them. This tests the algorithm's ability to find the true minimum among very similar values.

examples.title: Sparsely Packed Bus Stops
examples.why_included: With large gaps between stops, the optimal choice is usually more distinct and easier to find, serving as a sanity check.

examples.title: All Coordinates Negative (Except Stops)
examples.why_included: Ensures correct handling of negative coordinates for the university, which should be functionally identical to positive coordinates due to squaring in the distance formula.

examples.title: Optimal Stop is Second-to-Last
examples.why_included: A general case to ensure the loop logic is correct and doesn't have an off-by-one error when the optimum is near the end of the route.

examples.title: University at Large Negative X
examples.why_included: The bus moves in the positive x direction, away from the university. The student must get off at the first opportunity (stop 2).

examples.title: University at Large Positive X
examples.why_included: The university is far ahead on the route. The student should stay on the bus as long as possible to cover the large horizontal distance.

examples.title: Equal Bus and Student Speeds
examples.why_included: A special case where `vb == vs`. The function to minimize is proportional to `x_i + sqrt((xu-xi)^2 + yu^2)`. This tests the handling of this specific mathematical form.
